text: You get an array, stones, of weights. Each turn, take the two heaviest stones and smash them. Call them x and y, with x at most y. If they're equal, both are gone. If not, x is gone and y becomes y minus x. At the end there's at most one stone. Return its weight, or zero if none is left.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every turn I must pick the two heaviest stones, not any two. And the new stone, y minus x, goes back into the pile, so it can be picked again in a later turn. Is that right?

Then two things I notice right away. First, every turn removes at least one stone — two go in, and at most one comes out. So the game always ends, in at most n minus one turns. Second, there's a parity rule. y minus x and y plus x are always both even or both odd, so each smash keeps the parity of the total weight. The answer has the same parity as the sum — a nice quick sanity check. Are there any constraints on the input size?
There are between one and thirty stones, and each weight is between one and a thousand.

Got it. So there's at least one stone, and every weight is positive. Let me run through the example: two, seven, four, one, eight, one. Smashing eight and seven leaves a one, and the turns keep going until one stone of weight one is left. The sum is twenty-three, which is odd, so an odd answer fits the parity rule. And a single stone, like just one, has no turns at all, so the answer is one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to sort the stones every turn, take the two biggest, and put the difference back. It's correct, and with only thirty stones it's even fast enough, but it's n squared log n, re-sorting the whole list just to find two items. A trap here is to sort only once: the new stone can land anywhere in the order, so appending it at the end gives wrong answers — one, one, three returns minus one. This problem reminds me of a repeated take-the-maximum simulation, which is exactly what a max-heap does. The top is always the heaviest stone, and popping and pushing are log n each.

Here's the plan. One: build a max-heap from all the stones. Two: while at least two stones remain, pop the heaviest and the second heaviest, and if they differ, push back the difference. Three: return the last stone, or zero if the heap is empty. One thing worth flagging — the loop condition is size greater than one, not not-empty. Each turn pops two stones, so with a loop on not-empty and a single stone, the second pop runs on an empty heap — a crash or undefined behavior. The same goes for the return: one, one ends with zero stones, so I must check the size before calling top. A count array of size one thousand and one would also work, but with at most thirty stones, the heap is simpler. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. By default, priority queue in C++ is a max-heap, which is what I want, and building it from the iterator range heapifies in linear time instead of n pushes. The loop pops two, pushes the difference if they differ, and the return checks the size. One thing worth flagging — in my code, x is the heavier stone and y is the lighter one. That's the opposite of the names in the problem, so I push x minus y, not y minus x. Mixing them up pushes a negative number: one, two returns minus one. Also, when the two are equal I push nothing; pushing a zero would still be correct, just extra rounds.

Let's dry-run the code. Two, seven, four, one, eight, one — expected one. The row that matters is the first: eight and seven leave a one, and it sinks to the bottom of the heap while four becomes the new top. That's why I need a heap: the new stone doesn't stay at the end. Later, one and one are equal, so both vanish and the size drops by two, leaving one stone of weight one. That matches. Corner cases: one, one empties the heap, and the size check returns zero. One, two returns one — a min-heap or pushing y minus x gives minus one. Thirty stones of a thousand cancel in pairs, fifteen turns, answer zero.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is n log n: heapify is linear, each turn does at most two pops and one push, so log n, and there are at most n minus one turns, because each one removes at least one stone. Space is linear for the heap, which never grows beyond the starting n stones. The worst case is when each turn removes only one stone, so n minus one turns. Oh, one more thing — this copies the stones into a new heap, so the input is left alone. If changing the input was fine, I could run make heap on stones itself and save the extra linear memory.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that every turn removes at least one stone, which bounds the loop at n minus one, and you gave a parity check for free. You explained why the loop needs size greater than one and why the return needs a size check, each with a tiny input. And you caught that your x and y are swapped from the problem's names, and showed what goes wrong with y minus x. Good work.
